newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Tarkett, Sommer merge floor business.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tarkett, Sommer merge floor business.

text.p: Germany's Tarkett AG and French plastics group Sommer Allibert SA said on Wednesday they will merge their floor covering businesses to create one of the world's largest companies in the sector.

The deal involves Sommer-Allibert taking a 60 percent stake in Tarkett which in return will pay 705 million marks ($414 million) in cash for Sommer's floor covering business. Tarkett's payment will largely be financed by debt.
The news sent Tarkett's shares surging 20 percent or 6.40 marks to close at 38.50 marks. Sommer-Allibert's shares were trading down 3.2 percent at 210.50 francs in afternoon trade.
The merger will create a company called Tarkett-Sommer AG with annual sales of 2.6 billion marks, 27 plants worldwide and 8,800 employees.
Tarkett chief executive Lars Wisen said the link-up would boost profits of the merged group by 70 to 100 million marks annually after three years.
The drive for synergy benefits which may entail factory closures as capacity utilisation in the group's 19 factories in Europe was low at 75 percent.

"This is a perfect fit," Wisen, who will also head the merged group, told a presentation to bankers and reporters in Frankfurt. The merger opened up big opportunities to rationalise production and cooperate on distribution, he said.
The transaction has yet to be approved by competition authorites and by the company's supervisory boards and shareholders and Wisen said he expected it to go through in the final quarter of 1997.
He said the new group would be the number one worldwide in the production of hard flooring and would be the European market leader in all types of flooring.
BHF-Bank analyst Uwe Weinreich welcomed the move as strengthening Tarkett's earnings in the long term but recommended selling the shares now to take profits.

"It's certainly good news because production capacity in Europe will be concentrated but the real synergy benefits won't affect earnings until 1999," Weinreich said. "Today's share price rise was justified but I would now take profits."
Standard & Poor's credit agency said it may downgrade Tarkett because the deal would weaken Tarkett's financial structure and raise the level of net debt to capital to 74 percent from 33 percent.
The agency said it had placed Tarkett on CreditWatch with negative implications. Tarkett is currently rated BBB for corporate credit and BBB- for subordinated debt.
Under the deal, Sommer Allibert will buy 20.1 million shares or 60 percent of Tarkett through a public takeover offer of 32.75 marks per share.
The purchase will result in a significant cut in the 65 percent stake in Tarkett owned by investment funds affiliated to Doughty Hanson and Goldman Sachs Capital Partners.

Wisen said he did not expect outside shareholders, who own the remaining 35 percent of Tarkett's capital, to take up the offer because the price was too low to reflect the full value of Tarkett-Sommer.
Tarkett said it planned to finance the 705 million-mark payment by taking up 504 million in debt and by issuing a subordinated five-year warrant bond for 201 million marks.
It will also assume existing debt of approximately 250 million marks now owed by Sommer Allibert's flooring business.
After the warrants on Tarket-Sommer shares have been exercised, Sommer Allibert's stake in the merged group will be diluted to 50 percent. Wisen said Sommer did not intend to increase that stake.
($ = 1.702 German Marks)
